rows.unitTitle: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
rows.objective: Decide whether described conduct makes a person a broker who must hold a Texas licence, by applying the consideration clause and the twelve enumerated acts of Occupations Code § 1101.002(1)(A), the brokerage-as-status rule and business carve-outs of § 1101.004, the conditional wholesaling exemption in § 1101.0045, the persons and transactions listed in § 1101.005 with their qualifiers attached, the licence requirement in § 1101.351, and 22 TAC §§ 535.4 and 535.5 — and say for each answer whether the statute or a Commission rule supplies it.
rows.judgement: Whether an unpaid person who performed one enumerated act for another is inside the statutory definition of a broker.

rows.unitTitle: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
rows.objective: Decide whether described conduct makes a person a broker who must hold a Texas licence, by applying the consideration clause and the twelve enumerated acts of Occupations Code § 1101.002(1)(A), the brokerage-as-status rule and business carve-outs of § 1101.004, the conditional wholesaling exemption in § 1101.0045, the persons and transactions listed in § 1101.005 with their qualifiers attached, the licence requirement in § 1101.351, and 22 TAC §§ 535.4 and 535.5 — and say for each answer whether the statute or a Commission rule supplies it.
rows.judgement: That the wholesaling exemption is conditional, and that dropping its written disclosure makes the same conduct brokerage.

rows.objective: State what a failure of agency practice costs a Texas license holder, citing § 1101.003(a)(1) for why agency law is the first qualifying course, § 1101.652(b)(7) for the agency-specific disciplinary ground, § 1101.702(a) for the $5,000-per-violation ceiling with its per-day multiplier, § 1101.801 for the parallelism of the disciplinary, civil and criminal tracks, and §§ 1101.756 and 1101.758 for the criminal grade — and compute an unlicensed person's combined statutory exposure on a stated fee under § 1101.753(a) and § 1101.754(a).
rows.judgement: That the civil penalty for unlicensed brokerage is measured against the money received and is available twice, to the State and to the aggrieved person.

rows.objective: State what a failure of agency practice costs a Texas license holder, citing § 1101.003(a)(1) for why agency law is the first qualifying course, § 1101.652(b)(7) for the agency-specific disciplinary ground, § 1101.702(a) for the $5,000-per-violation ceiling with its per-day multiplier, § 1101.801 for the parallelism of the disciplinary, civil and criminal tracks, and §§ 1101.756 and 1101.758 for the criminal grade — and compute an unlicensed person's combined statutory exposure on a stated fee under § 1101.753(a) and § 1101.754(a).
rows.judgement: That a Commission order settles nothing in the other two tracks.

rows.unitTitle: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
rows.objective: Identify the role each person occupies in a Texas transaction — party under § 1101.551(2), principal or client, the broker as the party's agent under § 1101.557(a), the sales agent acting for that broker under §§ 1101.002(7) and 1101.351(c), the associated broker, the intermediary under § 1101.551(1), and the customer — state that TRELA defines neither "client" nor "customer", and list what a license holder owes a person the license holder does not represent under 22 TAC § 531.2, 22 TAC § 535.156(b) and (d) and § 1101.652(b)(3) and (b)(4).
rows.judgement: Who counts as a party under the statute's own definition, and that a license holder representing a party is expressly excluded from it.

rows.objective: Explain how a principal–agent relationship is created and what it demands: contrast the duties that follow from representation under § 1101.557(a) with the signed writing § 1101.806(c) requires before a commission can be sued for, state the fiduciary standard in 22 TAC § 531.2 and the boundaries drawn by 22 TAC § 537.11(b) and § 1101.556, apply the net-listing conditions in 22 TAC § 535.16(b), and describe the second principal–agent relationship — sales agent to sponsoring broker — under §§ 1101.351(c), 1101.803 and 1101.367(a).
rows.judgement: The asymmetry between conduct that creates agency duties and the signed writing that creates an enforceable commission claim.

rows.objective: Explain how a principal–agent relationship is created and what it demands: contrast the duties that follow from representation under § 1101.557(a) with the signed writing § 1101.806(c) requires before a commission can be sued for, state the fiduciary standard in 22 TAC § 531.2 and the boundaries drawn by 22 TAC § 537.11(b) and § 1101.556, apply the net-listing conditions in 22 TAC § 535.16(b), and describe the second principal–agent relationship — sales agent to sponsoring broker — under §§ 1101.351(c), 1101.803 and 1101.367(a).

rows.objective: State from Occupations Code § 1101.557(a) the two acts that make a broker a party's agent, explain why the status attaches to the broker rather than to the sales agent under §§ 1101.002(7) and 1101.351(c), and distinguish agency from compensation, from holding a licence and from friendliness — using § 1101.562(a)(1)'s exclusion of an oral agreement to show that representation can arise without a signed writing.
rows.judgement: That the representation relationship the statute recognises runs to the broker, with the sales agent acting for that broker.

rows.objective: State from Occupations Code § 1101.557(a) the two acts that make a broker a party's agent, explain why the status attaches to the broker rather than to the sales agent under §§ 1101.002(7) and 1101.351(c), and distinguish agency from compensation, from holding a licence and from friendliness — using § 1101.562(a)(1)'s exclusion of an oral agreement to show that representation can arise without a signed writing.
rows.judgement: That a duty owed to a party is not discharged by telling that party's license holder.

rows.objective: Trace a Texas sales agent's authority from the client to the broker to the agent, quoting the three rules in the three sentences of 22 TAC § 535.2(a) — written scope, written limitation or revocation, and the broker's responsibility for permitted acts beyond scope — and decide from § 1101.557(c)(1), § 1101.652(b)(18)–(20) and 22 TAC § 535.146(b) whether a proposed act is within express or implied actual authority or exceeds it.
rows.judgement: That a written scope protects a broker only while the broker enforces it, and that a limitation on scope must itself be written.

rows.objective: Trace a Texas sales agent's authority from the client to the broker to the agent, quoting the three rules in the three sentences of 22 TAC § 535.2(a) — written scope, written limitation or revocation, and the broker's responsibility for permitted acts beyond scope — and decide from § 1101.557(c)(1), § 1101.652(b)(18)–(20) and 22 TAC § 535.146(b) whether a proposed act is within express or implied actual authority or exceeds it.

rows.judgement: What the 2026 repeal of the two TRELA subagency references does and does not establish on the held sources.
controllingSources: Texas Occupations Code §§ 1101.002(8) and 1101.805(f), each shown as repealed by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1172 (S.B. 1968), Sec. 13, eff. January 1, 2026; TREC guidance on the 2026 changes, identified in the curriculum as guidance rather than law.
